unit.title: Persuasion and consumer psychology
unit.description: Cialdini principles, loss aversion, anchoring, framing, peak-end rule, choice overload, social proof, ethics of persuasion

cards.definition: Seven levers from Robert Cialdini: reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity, and unity (shared identity, added in 2016).
cards.example: A free audit (reciprocity), 2,000 clients served (social proof), places left this month (scarcity).

cards.definition: People look at what others like them do to decide, especially when they are unsure. Reviews, customer counts and testimonials work best when the others look similar to the buyer.
cards.example: Rated 4.7 by 3,200 parents converts parents better than a quote from a celebrity.

cards.definition: Interface tricks that push users against their interest: fake countdowns, hidden costs, hard-to-find cancellation, pre-ticked boxes. Banned by the EU Digital Services Act and consumer law, and they destroy trust.
cards.example: A timer that restarts at 10 minutes each time the page reloads.

exercises.prompt: A consultant offers a free audit, then proposes a paid plan. Which principle does the free audit use?
exercises.explain: People feel the need to return a favour. The gift must be genuinely useful, or it backfires.

exercises.prompt: Stop losing 200 euros a month works better than Save 200 euros a month. Why?
choices: Loss aversion: losses weigh more than equal gains
The anchoring effect of the 200 euro figure
The decoy effect between two offers
People prefer negative words in general
exercises.explain: Kahneman and Tversky showed losses weigh roughly twice as much as gains of the same size.

exercises.prompt: A crossed-out 120 euros next to 79 euros makes the price look smaller. Which bias?
exercises.explain: The first number seen becomes the reference. In France the crossed-out price must be a real former price.

exercises.prompt: Yoghurt sold as 95 percent fat-free instead of 5 percent fat uses which effect?
exercises.explain: Same fact, different frame, different choice. Framing is everywhere in copywriting.

exercises.prompt: Showing 3 plans instead of 12 often raises sales. Why?
choices: Choice overload makes people delay or give up
Fewer plans always lower the price paid
The law caps the number of plans
Customers only read the first three
exercises.explain: Too many options increase effort and fear of choosing wrong. Simplify and highlight a recommended choice.

exercises.prompt: A course ends with a strong final session and a certificate ceremony. Which principle does it use?
exercises.explain: People judge an experience by its best moment and its end, not by the average.

exercises.prompt: Which testimonial convinces small bakery owners best?
choices: A bakery owner from a similar town with real numbers
A famous chef who never ran a small shop
An anonymous quote with no name or photo
The founder praising their own product
exercises.explain: Social proof works best when the others look like the buyer. Specific numbers add credibility.

exercises.prompt: A countdown timer that restarts each time the page is reloaded is an acceptable growth tactic.
exercises.explain: False. A fake urgency is a dark pattern and a misleading commercial practice. It can bring fines and destroys trust once noticed.

exercises.prompt: Asking for a small yes (a free trial) before a big yes (a yearly plan) uses which principle?
exercises.explain: People like to act in line with what they already did. Small first steps raise later conversion.

exercises.prompt: Which use of scarcity is honest?
choices: Only 20 seats because the workshop is run live by one trainer
Only 3 left shown on every product, whatever the stock
A price that ends tonight, every night of the year
Limited edition on a product made in endless runs
exercises.explain: Scarcity is ethical when it is true. Fake scarcity is illegal in France and burns the brand once spotted.
